questions.question: What is the primary purpose of inferential statistics in psychological research?

answers.text: To calculate descriptive summary data for samples
To use sample statistics to draw conclusions about population parameters
To eliminate all sampling error from research studies
To prove that the null hypothesis is always false

questions.question: What does sampling error refer to in inferential statistics?

answers.text: Mistakes made by researchers when collecting data
Random variability in a statistic from sample to sample
Errors caused by using non-random sampling methods
Systematic bias in measurement instruments

questions.question: What does the null hypothesis (H₀) represent in null hypothesis testing?

answers.text: There is a strong relationship in the population
The sample relationship occurred by chance and there is no relationship in the population
The alternative hypothesis must be true
The researcher has made an error in data collection

questions.question: What is the conventional alpha (α) level used in null hypothesis testing?
What is the most common misinterpretation of the p value?

answers.text: That it represents the strength of the relationship between variables
That it is the probability that the null hypothesis is true
That it must always be less than .05 to be meaningful
That it is calculated incorrectly by statistical software

questions.question: According to Table 13.1, which combination of relationship strength and sample size would result in a statistically significant finding for both Cohen's d and Pearson's r?

answers.text: Weak relationship with small sample (N = 20)
Medium relationship with medium sample (N = 50)
Weak relationship with medium sample (N = 50)
Strong relationship with small sample (N = 20) for Cohen's d only

questions.question: What is the key difference between statistical significance and practical significance?

answers.text: Statistical significance is always more important than practical significance
Practical significance refers to the importance or usefulness of a result in real-world contexts
They are essentially the same concept with different names
Practical significance can only be determined with large sample sizes

questions.question: What type of t-test would be used to compare the mean number of depressive symptoms in a sample of 50 adults with clinical depression to a hypothetical population mean?

answers.text: Independent-samples t-test
One-sample t-test
Dependent-samples t-test
Factorial t-test

questions.question: In a dependent-samples t-test, what is the first step in the analysis?

answers.text: Calculate the correlation between the two sets of scores
Reduce the two scores for each participant to a single difference score
Compare the means of two separate groups
Determine if the variances are equal

questions.question: What does a two-tailed test evaluate compared to a one-tailed test?

answers.text: Whether the sample mean differs from the hypothetical population mean in a specific predicted direction only
Whether the sample mean differs from the hypothetical population mean in either direction
Whether two independent samples differ from each other
Whether the correlation is positive or negative

questions.question: What does the F statistic in an ANOVA represent?

answers.text: The correlation between the independent and dependent variables
The ratio of mean squares between groups to mean squares within groups
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The effect size of the relationship

questions.question: Why are post hoc comparisons conducted after a statistically significant one-way ANOVA?

answers.text: To increase the statistical power of the analysis
To determine which specific group means differ from each other
To calculate the effect size of the overall difference
To verify that the ANOVA was calculated correctly

questions.question: What is a Type I error in null hypothesis testing?

answers.text: Retaining the null hypothesis when it is false
Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Failing to collect enough data for adequate power
Using the wrong statistical test for the research design

questions.question: What is a Type II error in null hypothesis testing?

answers.text: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Retaining the null hypothesis when it is false
Calculating the p value incorrectly
Using a one-tailed test when a two-tailed test is appropriate

questions.question: What does the file drawer problem refer to in psychological research?

answers.text: Researchers losing their data due to poor organization
The tendency for non-significant results to not be submitted or accepted for publication
The difficulty of accessing archived research materials
Ethical violations in data storage practices

questions.question: What is statistical power in research design?

answers.text: The probability of correctly retaining a true null hypothesis
The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis given the sample size and expected relationship strength
The strength of the correlation between variables
The likelihood of committing a Type I error

questions.question: What is the common guideline for adequate statistical power?
What is p-hacking?

answers.text: A legitimate method for increasing statistical power
Making various decisions in the research process to artificially achieve a statistically significant result
A technique for calculating p values more accurately
A software program for conducting null hypothesis tests

questions.question: What does a 95% confidence interval around a statistic indicate?

answers.text: That 95% of the sample falls within that range
That there is a 95% chance the population parameter lies within that range
That the null hypothesis will be rejected 95% of the time
That the statistical power is .95

questions.question: What is one of the key features of open science practices in response to the replicability crisis?

answers.text: Keeping research methods secret to prevent competitors from replicating studies
Pre-registering hypotheses and sharing raw data and research materials
Publishing only statistically significant findings
Eliminating the use of null hypothesis testing entirely
